title: Trial of Socrates for Impiety and Corrupting Youth
description: The trial of Socrates in Athens (399 BCE) on charges of impiety (asebeia) and corrupting the youth of the city established an important precedent for the prosecution of unconventional religious and philosophical thought. Socrates was accused of introducing new divinities and denying the traditional gods, charges that blend religious heterodoxy with social danger. His execution by hemlock poisoning demonstrates the Athenian polis's willingness to deploy the death penalty against perceived religious transgression. This case is analyzed by scholars as an early instance of the pattern linking intellectual non-conformity with dangerous supernatural association.
historiographical_note: Classicists including M.I. Finley and Robin Lane Fox have examined the Socrates trial as a case study in the policing of religious boundaries, relevant to later patterns of heresy and witchcraft prosecution.
source_method: Published scholarship; primary sources (Plato's Apology, Xenophon's Memorabilia)
